newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania starts crime debate before Orthodox Easter.
newsitem.headline: Romania starts crime debate before Orthodox Easter.

text.p: Romanians alarmed at an upsurge in street crime launched a public debate on Friday to persuade authorities to determine who was responsible for the violence and to toughen the justice system.

Two days before the country's most hallowed religious holiday, Orthodox Easter, commentators urged the government to divert its attention from an anti-corruption crusade and take steps to allow its citizens to walk the street unmolested.

"Society is frightened by the unprecedented rise of violence, by the explosion of crime which leaves us exposed and helpless in the face of barbarism," the independent daily Adevarul said. "Most serious is an irresponsible justice system making concessions to criminals with records."
The campaign was triggered by a series of brutal incidents leading up to weekend candlelit Easter services supposed to be given over to reflection and upholding public morals.

A popular television presenter was seriously injured when attacked by armed burglars in his home. Viewers also saw the body of a man on a pavement, abandoned by an ambulance crew unable to get him admitted at three hospitals.

Other incidents included an attack in broad daylight on two journalists in the Transylvanian town of Brasov and the attempted robbery of a shop assistant in the same town by a gang firing in the air and brandishing a grenade.

Like all countries in eastern Europe, Romania has faced increased crime since the fall of communism in 1989, but gangland murders and protection rackets have generally been less prominent than in neighbouring states.

Reformist President Emil Constantinescu, elected last November, sees his main goal as rooting out corruption among officials and businessmen he blames for stunting market reforms and allowing a shadow economy to flourish.
But commentators said the concerns of ordinary Romanians also lay elsewhere -- in day-to-day safety.

"We must change our attitude and goals," urged the daily Evenimentul Zilei. "Otherwise we may get order in the economy but will no longer be able to walk the streets and will have to barricade ourselves in our homes."
Speaking to reporters after visiting the injured television presenter in hospital, Constantinescu said lurid media coverage was at least partly to blame for increased street violence.
"The media should also think twice about what is being printed and put on television screens," he said. "Newspapers resort to all sorts of things to increase sales."
Justice Minister Valeriu Stoica also blamed the media but urged judges to impose tougher sentences on repeat offenders.

"Certainly some judges are to blame for how they ruled in cases involving hardened offenders, but the media has also its share of guilt for the rise of violence," Stoica told a talk show early on Friday.
